description: Solo engineering research and pipeline development for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. Team roster is closed; not accepting external members.
summary:
**Project Kugelblitz Vanguard** is an astronomical data-analysis platform developed for NASA's Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. It aims to make multi-epoch astronomical observations easier to analyse by identifying meaningful changes in the sky across different observations.

The platform processes SPHEREx observational data, compares compatible observations across different epochs, and analyses variations in detected astronomical sources. By combining image-processing techniques, computational analysis, and machine learning, it helps identify potentially interesting astronomical phenomena while reducing the need for repetitive manual inspection.

Our solution focuses on building an accessible, interactive web interface that brings complex astronomical data and analytical results together in one place. The goal is to make large-scale astronomical datasets more interpretable and help users investigate changes in the universe more efficiently.

By connecting NASA's scientific datasets with modern computational tools, Kugelblitz Vanguard demonstrates how data-driven approaches can support astronomical exploration.
details:
1. Project Overview

SPHEREx Epoch Lab is an astronomical data-analysis platform developed for NASA's Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. It enables users to investigate how regions of the infrared sky change over time by comparing SPHEREx observations from different epochs.

A major challenge in comparing SPHEREx observations is that the instrument samples 102 infrared spectral bands, and a source's position on the detector can affect the wavelength measured across different observations. Directly subtracting incompatible images can therefore produce misleading signals that resemble genuine astronomical variability.

Our project addresses this problem by prioritising scientifically compatible observations before performing image comparisons.

2. How It Works

The platform follows a four-stage workflow:

A. Target Selection and Data Retrieval

Users can select a predefined astronomical target, search by object name, or enter celestial coordinates (RA/Dec). The backend retrieves relevant SPHEREx DR1 observations and associated calibration products through NASA/IPAC's Infrared Science Archive (IRSA).

B. Observation Matching and Calibration

The system identifies observation pairs with overlapping sky coverage and compatible wavelength responses. It uses SPHEREx calibration maps, including CWAVE and CBAND products, to evaluate wavelength compatibility. Observations that fail required calibration or compatibility checks are excluded rather than silently compared.

C. Image Processing and Comparison

Compatible observations undergo astrometric alignment, point-spread-function matching, background modelling and uncertainty propagation. The resulting images can be compared through overlays, blinking visualisations and statistically significant difference maps.

The system also performs source detection, association and motion analysis to distinguish potentially meaningful astronomical changes from instrumental or processing artefacts.

D. Results and Scientific Verification

Users can inspect detected residuals, source measurements, uncertainty estimates and validation results. Outputs are available in FITS, JSON, CSV and PNG formats, allowing results to be independently examined and reproduced.

3. Data Sources and Technologies

The project uses:

  • NASA/IPAC IRSA: SPHEREx DR1 observations and FITS image cutouts.
  • IRSA DataLink: Observation-specific CWAVE and CBAND calibration products.
  • ESA Gaia DR3: Reference stars and astrometric associations.
  • NASA/JPL Horizons: Observer position vectors used in parallax calculations.

The scientific processing pipeline is written in Python, with FastAPI providing the backend and a JavaScript-based web interface providing user interaction.

The system also maintains cached observations, checkpoints and file fingerprints to support reproducibility and offline inspection of previously recorded analyses.

4. Testing and Results

The project has been evaluated using real SPHEREx observations rather than relying exclusively on simulated demonstrations.

One validated comparison examined the Barnard field across observations separated by 31 days, within the 0.83–0.86 µm wavelength range.

  • 23,265 matched pixels were evaluated.
  • 909 stars were used to calibrate the source-noise model.
  • 27 out of 31 injected synthetic sources with signal-to-noise ratios of 10 were recovered at a 5σ detection threshold.
  • All five validation gates passed.
  • No independently verified astronomical change was identified in this field.

A second analysis examined Epsilon Indi B across five epochs at 1.107 µm over approximately one year. Its measured motion was detected at 11.3σ and agreed with the catalogue proper-motion measurement within 1.1σ.

The saved scientific products also underwent 84 independent verification checks, with 81 passing, zero failing and three remaining unverified because the available observations could not establish those particular capabilities. The software test suite contains 270 passing tests.

5. Innovation and Intended Impact

The central innovation of SPHEREx Epoch Lab is its emphasis on wavelength-aware temporal comparison rather than straightforward image subtraction.

By incorporating calibration-aware observation selection, uncertainty modelling, astrometric alignment and traceable scientific outputs, the platform aims to reduce false-positive detections and make multi-epoch infrared observations more accessible.

Its intended impact is to provide researchers, students and astronomy enthusiasts with a reproducible way to investigate changes in the infrared sky, examine candidate astronomical phenomena and explore the scientific potential of SPHEREx observations.

6. Limitations and Future Development

The current implementation has limitations, including archive availability, saturated astronomical sources and insufficient wavelength overlap between some observations. Sensitivity to known variable stars still requires further validation using suitable unsaturated targets.

The project does not claim a new Planet X discovery or a confirmed astronomical transient. Its purpose is to provide a scientifically controlled framework for investigating such possibilities, with candidate detections requiring independent verification.
